title: Traffic Light Controlled Intersection
statement:
On LeetCode this is a multithreading problem in which every car is a thread. Here every car is an asynchronous task, and you coordinate the tasks with promises.

Two roads cross at an intersection. Road A (`roadId = 1`) carries traffic north to south (direction 1) and south to north (direction 2); road B (`roadId = 2`) carries traffic west to east (direction 3) and east to west (direction 4). Each road has its own traffic light, and exactly one of the two lights is green at any moment, starting with road A. While a road's light is green its cars may cross in either direction; while it is red they must wait.

Write a class `TrafficLight` with one method, `carArrived(carId, roadId, direction, turnGreen, crossCar)`. A single instance serves every car, and each car calls the method once when it reaches the intersection. The two callbacks act for that car:

- `turnGreen()` makes this car's road green (and the other road red) at once, and prints `"Traffic Light On Road A Is Green"` or `"Traffic Light On Road B Is Green"`.
- `crossCar()` drives the car into the intersection, prints `"Car <carId> Has Passed Road <A or B> In Direction <direction>"`, and returns a promise that resolves once the car has left the intersection.

Every car must cross exactly once, and these rules must hold:

- A car enters only while its own road is green.
- The light changes only while the intersection is empty, so cars of the two roads are never in it together.
- `turnGreen()` is never called while its road is already green.
- No car waits needlessly: crossing takes no measurable time, so each car crosses in the same millisecond it arrives. Wait on promises, not on timers.

Each case gives `cars`, `directions` and `arrivalTimes`: car `cars[i]` arrives at `arrivalTimes[i]` ms heading in direction `directions[i]`, and its road follows from that direction. Cars that arrive at the same time call `carArrived` in index order. The answer is the list of printed lines, in order. Cars that arrive at the same moment may cross in any order, so every answer that keeps the rules is accepted.
constraints: The values of cars are distinct integers from 1 to 1000
signature: List<String> TrafficLight(int[] cars, int[] directions, int[] arrivalTimes)
api: class TrafficLight { carArrived(carId: number, roadId: number, direction: number, turnGreen: () => void, crossCar: () => Promise<void>): void | Promise<void> }

notes:
## Intuition

The light is shared state, and every car does a check-then-act on it: look at the light, switch it if needed, drive through. With threads, another car can slip in between the check and the act. JavaScript never interrupts synchronous code, but a car stays in the intersection across `await crossCar()`, and during that pause other cars' tasks run. So a car's whole visit (check, switch, enter, leave) must be a critical section that one car holds at a time. A chain of promises gives exactly that: a first-come, first-served lock in which each car's turn starts when the previous turn has finished. (The brute force builds the same lock by hand, with a waiting list and a `busy` flag.)

## Approach

1. `greenRoad` remembers the green road (1 at the start); `lastTurn` is the promise of the latest car's turn, already resolved at first.
2. When a car arrives, chain its `turn` after `lastTurn` with `then`.
3. In its turn, if `greenRoad` is not `roadId`, call `turnGreen()` and record the new road. The previous car has left, so the intersection is empty.
4. Await `crossCar()`, so the turn ends only after the car has left.
5. Store `turn` in `lastTurn` so the next car waits for it.

With threads the same design is a mutex: a `synchronized` method, or `lock.lock()`, then the light check, `turnGreen` and `crossCar`, then `lock.unlock()` in a `finally`. A semaphore with one permit works too. Acquiring the lock plays the part of waiting for `lastTurn`, and releasing it the part of `turn` resolving.

## Example 1, step by step

- Cars 1, 3 and 5 are on road A and arrive at 10, 20 and 30 ms. `greenRoad` is 1, so each one crosses without touching the light.
- Car 2 arrives at 40 ms on road B. `greenRoad` is 1, so it calls `turnGreen()`, sets `greenRoad = 2` and crosses.
- Car 4 arrives at 50 ms, also on road B, and crosses at once.
- The answer is three road A crossings, the road B light, then cars 2 and 4.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1) work per car.
- Space: O(k) for the k cars whose turns are chained and waiting at the same moment.

## Pitfalls

- Checking the light outside the turn, or not awaiting `crossCar()`: a car of the other road arriving in the same millisecond switches the light while the first car is still inside.
- Calling `turnGreen()` for a road that is already green is a wrong answer, so compare with `greenRoad` first.
- Polling with `setTimeout` makes cars cross late; wait on the previous turn's promise.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `greenRoad` | the road whose light is green: 1 for A, 2 for B |
| `lastTurn` | promise of the most recent car's turn; the next turn starts after it |
| `turn` | this car's turn: switch the light if needed, cross, wait until the car has left |

narration.4: An already resolved promise: the first car does not have to wait for anybody.
narration.8: Chain this car's turn after the previous car's turn, so only one car at a time is between the check and leaving.
narration.9: Inside its turn the car looks at the light; nobody else can change it now.
narration.10: Its road is red, so turn it green; the previous car has already left the intersection.
narration.11: Remember the new green road for the cars that follow.
narration.13: Cross and wait until the car has left the intersection before the turn ends.
narration.15: The next car to arrive will wait for this turn.
narration.16: Returning the turn lets the caller know when this car is through.
